explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says they heard the antichrist is coming, and then he adds that "now many antichrists have appeared." He doesn't say it's one lonely figure way off in the future. He says it's already happening, and that's how he knows it's the last hour (1 John 2:18).

Nothing about a capture here, friend. The writer says the believers heard the antichrist is coming, and then he says "now many antichrists have appeared." So the news is not one figure caught, it's many who have shown up. I think a capture would have made a much shorter letter (1 John 2:18).

No name gets handed out in this verse. The writer says they heard the antichrist is coming, and then he says "now many antichrists have appeared." So the news is about how many there are, not what anyone is called. No name tag, no seating chart (1 John 2:18).

Yes, baker. The writer says, "They went out from us, but they did not belong to us." So these antichrists were once around the believers, and then they left. That's the whole point of the verse (1 John 2:19).

Not quite, friend. The text really says the opposite: "They went out from us, but they did not belong to us." So they did go out from among the believers. Then the writer adds that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19).

That's it. The writer says, "For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us." Staying is how he describes belonging here. Their leaving made it clear that none of them belonged (1 John 2:19).

Worship is a good word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The writer says, "For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us." The word is about staying, not about what they did while they were there. I'll admit worshiped sounded holy enough to fit (1 John 2:19).

Serving is a fine thing, baker, but this verse doesn't use it. The writer says, "For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us." His point is about staying put. Their departure made it clear that none of them belonged (1 John 2:19).

All of them, baker. The writer tells the believers, "You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth." He doesn't pick out a smart few. That's good news for the whole batch (1 John 2:20).

Close, but the writer doesn't leave anybody out. He says, "You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth." Not most, ALL. Not one cookie left off the tray (1 John 2:20).

Some is too small, friend. The writer says, "You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth." He's speaking to every one of the believers, not a handful. That anointing comes from the Holy One (1 John 2:20).

Not this time, baker. The writer says he wrote "because no lie comes from the truth." So a lie and the truth don't come from the same place. The statement on the card says the opposite, so it's false (1 John 2:21).

Right. The writer says he wrote to them "because no lie comes from the truth." Truth doesn't produce lies, not even a little one. He's also telling the believers they already have the truth (1 John 2:21).

explanations.answer: Whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer asks, "Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" Then he says this is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. He answers his own question right there in the verse (1 John 2:22).

That's not who he points to, friend. The writer asks, "Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" His answer is about denying who Jesus is, not about a day of rest. Keep an eye on that question, because he answers it quick (1 John 2:22).

Good guess, but that's not the answer in the text. The writer says the liar is "the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ." He doesn't mention the prophets in this passage. His focus is on what people say about Jesus (1 John 2:22).
Not quite, baker. The writer says, "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father." So the card has it backward. Denying the Son and still having the Father don't go together here (1 John 2:23).

That's right. The writer says, "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well." The Father and the Son go together in this verse. You can't leave one at the counter and take the other home (1 John 2:23).

True, baker. The writer says, "As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you." That's their job, and he follows it with a promise. If it remains, they'll remain in the Son and in the Father (1 John 2:24).

Not this time, friend. The writer really does say it: "As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you." He wants that message to stay with them. And he says that if it does, they will also remain in the Son and in the Father (1 John 2:24).

Yes, baker. The writer says, "And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life." It's a promise that comes from Him, and the writer counts himself in with the believers when he says "to us" (1 John 2:25).

A land was promised to Abraham's family in the Old Testament (Genesis 12:7), but that's not the promise in this verse. The writer says, "And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life." So the answer here is eternal life, friend (1 John 2:25).

Peace sounds nice, baker, but it's not what the verse names. The writer says, "And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life." Nothing here about enemies at all. The promise is eternal life (1 John 2:25).

explanations.answer: Those who are trying to deceive them
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says, "I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you." So everything about the antichrists and the lies was written with those deceivers in mind. He's looking out for the believers (1 John 2:26).

explanations.answer: Those who are new to the faith
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. The writer says, "I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you." He's writing about the deceivers, not about newcomers. The new folks aren't mentioned in this verse (1 John 2:26).

explanations.answer: Those who are suffering for Jesus
explanations.explanation: Suffering is real, baker, but this verse isn't about it. The writer says, "I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you." The group is the deceivers, and that's who this whole passage has been about (1 John 2:26).

explanations.answer: Remain in Him as they were taught
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, "…so remain in Him as you have been taught." The anointing teaches them about all things, and he tells them to stay in Him. That's the same word he used for the message staying in them (1 John 2:27).

explanations.answer: Go bring back the ones who left
explanations.explanation: Good heart, baker, but the writer doesn't say that. He tells them, "…so remain in Him as you have been taught." Nothing in this verse sends them after the ones who left. The instruction is about staying in Him (1 John 2:27).

Teaching is a good thing, friend, but it's not what this verse says. The writer tells them, "…so remain in Him as you have been taught." He also says they don't need anyone to teach them, because His anointing teaches them. So the instruction is to remain in Him (1 John 2:27).
